name: Minimum spanning tree by agents

origin.note: MST in the agent-based model appeared together with leader election (DISC 2024).

summary: $n$ agents in an anonymous weighted graph must build a minimum spanning tree.
statement: $n$ agents with distinct identifiers are placed on the nodes of an anonymous port-labelled graph with $n$ nodes, $m$ edges and maximum degree $\Delta$ (rooted, dispersed, or arbitrary start). Agents compute only by moving and by talking when co-located. The agents must build a minimum spanning tree of the edge-weighted graph, each agent knowing which incident edges belong to it: every agent (or node) learns its part of the output. **Time** is in synchronous rounds; **memory** in bits per agent.

primer.intro: Imagine $n$ agents, one in each room of a building, who must choose which corridors to keep open so that every room can still reach every other, using the cheapest possible total length. The building is a graph with $n$ nodes (rooms), $m$ edges (corridors) and maximum degree $\Delta$; each edge has a weight (its cost), which the agents on its two ends can see, and the doors of a room are numbered (*ports*). A *spanning tree* is a set of $n-1$ edges that connects all nodes without forming a cycle, and a *minimum spanning tree* (MST) is one with the smallest total weight. In the basic version the agents start one per node (a *dispersed* start), have distinct IDs, move in synchronous *rounds* (talk to agents in the same room, then walk at most one corridor), and at the end every agent must know which of its own edges belong to the MST. We count rounds and bits of memory per agent. As for all problems in this family, the agents can imitate a message-passing algorithm by walking to their neighbours, the method explained under leader election by agents.

ideas.title: Grow fragments along their lightest outgoing edges
ideas.idea:
This is the classic Borůvka / Gallager-Humblet-Spira idea, carried out by agents. Assume all edge weights differ (agents can break ties using their IDs and port numbers).

1. At the start every node is its own *fragment* (a small tree).
2. In each phase, every agent meets its neighbours (using the ID-bit schedule, see leader election by agents) and learns which of its edges leave its fragment and how heavy they are.
3. The agents of each fragment pass the lightest such edge up their tree to the fragment's leader, which picks the lightest outgoing edge of the whole fragment.
4. Every fragment adds its lightest outgoing edge; fragments joined by these edges merge into one, with one leader.
5. Repeat until one fragment remains: it is the MST, and its leader is also an elected leader for all agents.
ideas.analysis: Step 4 is safe because of the *cut property*: the lightest edge leaving any group of nodes always belongs to the MST. Every fragment merges with at least one other in each phase, so the number of fragments at least halves, and $O(\log n)$ phases suffice. In total this gives $O(n\log n + \Delta\log^2 n)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits per agent, assuming the agents know $L$, the largest ID [Chand2025Trees]. The first agent algorithm handled the fragments one at a time and needed $O(m + n\log n)$ rounds and $O(n\log n)$ bits [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE].
ideas.why_it_matters: Halving the number of fragments in every phase is the standard way to build spanning trees in parallel, and the resulting tree gives agents a root and a structure for broadcasting, used afterwards for BFS and counting problems.

ideas.title: On a ring, the heaviest edge is far away
ideas.idea:
Information moves at most one edge per round, because it travels only inside agents and each agent walks at most one edge per round. So after $t$ rounds, what the agent on node $y$ knows depends only on the part of the graph within distance $t$ of $y$.

Take a ring of $n$ nodes with distinct weights. The MST of a ring is the ring minus its heaviest edge. Look at an edge $e = \{u, v\}$ and an edge $f$ on the opposite side of the ring, at distance about $n/2$ from $u$ and $v$. Give every edge other than $e$ and $f$ a weight below the weight of $e$. If $f$ is lighter than $e$, then $e$ is the heaviest edge and is not in the MST; if $f$ is heavier, $e$ is in the MST.
ideas.analysis: Within fewer than about $n/2 - 1$ rounds the agents on $u$ and $v$ cannot tell these two rings apart, so they answer the same way and one answer is wrong. Hence any algorithm needs $\Omega(n)$ rounds on a ring, and $\Omega(D)$ rounds in general, where $D$ is the diameter (largest distance between two nodes). This is our own short argument; the catalogue records no lower bound. On a ring $\Delta = 2$, so the best algorithm, $O(n\log n + \Delta\log^2 n)$, is within a $\log n$ factor of it there.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that an MST is a global object: an edge's membership can depend on an edge at the other end of the graph.

history: Spanning trees were the first application of agent-based leader election [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]; the question since has been **rounds, then memory**, without knowledge of graph parameters [Chand2025Trees].

axes.name: Knowledge

values.label: $n$ and $\Delta$ are known
values.definition: Every agent knows $n$ and $\Delta$ (upper bounds suffice where stated).

axes.origin: Whether agents know global parameters is inherited from message passing, where nodes typically know $n$ or an upper bound on it, and possibly $\Delta$ and $D$; Kshemkalyani, Kumar, Molla and Sharma set the agent-based model against this and asked for algorithms that rely on no such knowledge, "neither exact nor an upper bound" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Knowing $n$ and $\Delta$ tells an agent how long to wait: in the arbitrary-start minimal dominating set algorithm of Chand, Molla and Sivasubramaniam every robot waits $\kappa n\Delta$ rounds before leader election begins [Chand2023Cover], and the introductory maximal independent set algorithm assumes both $n$ and $\Delta$ [Pattanayak2024MIS] (as reported by [Kaur2026MIS] and [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]). Kshemkalyani et al. state the trade-off: solutions without knowledge "are more resilient to network changes and device faults", but "algorithm design becomes challenging since devices may not know how long to run a procedure to guarantee a solution" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Later papers remove the assumption by first dispersing with termination detection and electing a leader, after which a spanning tree lets the agents compute $\Delta$ and the largest identifier themselves [Chand2026Triangle]; knowing only that largest identifier $L$ is a weaker assumption, recorded on results rather than as a level of this axis [Chand2025Trees]. For minimum spanning trees, Kshemkalyani et al. need no parameter [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE], and Chand, Kumar and Molla reduce memory to $O(\log n)$ bits knowing only $L$ [Chand2025Trees].

variants.title: Dispersed start
variants.summary: From a dispersed start, an MST takes $O(n\log n+\Delta\log^2 n)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits.

figure.caption: MST by growing fragments along their lightest outgoing edges (Borůvka, Gallager-Humblet-Spira) [Chand2025Trees]: agents dispersed on a weighted cycle meet their neighbours with the ID-bit schedule (in each block of $2\Delta = 4$ rounds, agents whose current ID bit is 1 walk to each neighbour and back, one edge per round). Each one-node fragment adds its lightest edge (weights 1 and 2), giving two fragments (colours) with leaders 3 and 2 (circled). In phase 2 the agents meet again with the same walks (shown round by round) and find the edges that leave their fragment (red); 5 and 6 walk to their leaders to report the lightest outgoing edge, both fragments pick weight 3 and merge into the minimum spanning tree (thick).

frames.label: Start: dispersed; every node its own fragment
Each adds its lightest edge: fragments merge
Phase 2: edges 3 and 4 leave the fragments
Final: both pick edge 3; one fragment, the MST
